heading: Cold open
narration: Resting lets two physical processes finish after the heat is gone: heat keeps travelling inward from the hot outer layers, so the centre continues to cook, and the meat cools enough that less of its liquid runs out when it is cut.

heading: Cold open
narration: The USDA's temperature guidance for whole cuts of beef, pork, veal and lamb pairs 145 degrees Fahrenheit with a 3-minute rest, because the temperature holds or climbs during that time.

heading: Title card

heading: The heat is still moving when the pan goes cold
narration: Start with what the pan or oven actually does. Heat enters at the surface.

heading: The heat is still moving when the pan goes cold
narration: It travels inward by conduction, with each layer of meat warming the next.

heading: The heat is still moving when the pan goes cold
narration: That process is slow, because meat is mostly water and protein, and neither moves heat quickly.

heading: The heat is still moving when the pan goes cold
narration: So at any moment during cooking, a thick roast is not one temperature.

heading: The heat is still moving when the pan goes cold
narration: It has hot outer layers, a cooler centre, and a slope of temperatures running between them.

heading: The heat is still moving when the pan goes cold
narration: When you lift it out, nothing feeds the outside any more. The heat already stored in those outer layers does not vanish, though.

heading: The heat is still moving when the pan goes cold
narration: Some of it escapes into the air. The rest keeps flowing the only other way it can, inward and down the slope toward the cooler centre.

heading: The heat is still moving when the pan goes cold
narration: That is why a roast keeps cooking after it leaves the heat.

heading: The heat is still moving when the pan goes cold
narration: You do not have to take this on trust. The instrument is a probe thermometer in the centre, left in place after the meat comes off the heat.

heading: Cooking wrings water out of muscle fibres
narration: Now for the juice. Raw muscle is a bundle of long fibres, each one packed with protein filaments, and most of its weight is water held in and around them.

heading: Cooking wrings water out of muscle fibres
narration: As the meat heats, proteins in the fibres contract. They unfold, tangle and tighten, and the fibres shorten and narrow.

heading: Cooking wrings water out of muscle fibres
narration: Water is squeezed out, the way water leaves a sponge as you wring it.

heading: Cooking wrings water out of muscle fibres
narration: The connective tissue shrinks as well, wrapped around the bundles and tightening the squeeze.

heading: Cooking wrings water out of muscle fibres
narration: The released liquid collects between the fibres, in channels it did not fill before.

heading: Cooking wrings water out of muscle fibres
narration: Some of it reaches the surface and evaporates or drips. Some is still in the meat, loose, when you pick up the knife.

heading: Cooking wrings water out of muscle fibres
narration: You cannot see water inside a steak, so this has to be measured indirectly.

heading: Cooking wrings water out of muscle fibres
narration: One tool is low-field NMR, short for nuclear magnetic resonance. It uses the same physics as medical scanners, at a smaller scale.

heading: Cooking wrings water out of muscle fibres
narration: It listens to hydrogen in water molecules and reports how freely that water moves.

heading: Cooking wrings water out of muscle fibres
narration: Water bound tightly to protein, water trapped inside the fibres and water sitting loose between them each give a different signal.

heading: Cooking wrings water out of muscle fibres
narration: Meat scientists publishing in journals such as the Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry, from the American Chemical Society, have used it to follow cooking.

heading: Cooking wrings water out of muscle fibres
narration: As the meat heats, the signal from water inside the fibres shrinks and the signal from water between them grows.

heading: Cooking wrings water out of muscle fibres
narration: In other words, heating shifts water toward the free fraction, out of the fibres and into the gaps.

heading: Cooking wrings water out of muscle fibres
narration: This is mainstream science. Researchers at the USDA Agricultural Research Service study meat quality, including how much water a cut holds and loses.

heading: Cooking wrings water out of muscle fibres

heading: Cooking wrings water out of muscle fibres
narration: Across that literature the direction is consistent: more heat means more contraction, and more contraction pushes more liquid loose.

heading: Cooking wrings water out of muscle fibres
narration: The old kitchen explanation gets that part right. It goes wrong about what happens next.

heading: Juice is not herded into the centre
narration: The familiar version goes like this. A hot sear seals the surface, the heat drives the juice inward to the centre, and resting lets it spread back out to the edges so the slice stays moist.

narration: So the popular story scores unevenly. The claim that liquid is squeezed loose by heat is supported.

heading: Juice is not herded into the centre
narration: The claim that a sear seals the surface is not. The claim that juice is herded into the centre and flows back is unproven at best, and nothing else in the explanation depends on it.

heading: Juice is not herded into the centre

narration: Then cut it and weigh what runs onto the board. Do that for pieces sliced at once and pieces left to rest, and you have numbers instead of impressions.

heading: A scale tests what a story cannot
narration: Meat sliced straight away sheds more onto the board than meat that has rested.

heading: A scale tests what a story cannot
narration: That difference is real. Resting meat is not sealed either, though. While it sits, it stays hot, keeps steaming and drips a little onto the plate.

heading: A scale tests what a story cannot
narration: Some of the water that would have reached the board goes into the air instead.

heading: A scale tests what a story cannot
narration: As a result, the total loss of a rested piece is often closer to that of an unrested piece than the puddle suggests.

heading: A scale tests what a story cannot
narration: How close depends on the cut and the conditions, and published comparisons do not agree on a single figure. Resting shrinks the puddle more clearly than it shrinks the total.

heading: Cooler juice runs out more slowly
narration: So why does less run out of rested meat? The best-supported answer concerns the liquid itself.

heading: Cooler juice runs out more slowly
narration: Meat juice is not plain water. It carries dissolved proteins, along with gelatin from connective tissue.

heading: Cooler juice runs out more slowly
narration: Its viscosity, meaning how strongly a liquid resists flowing, rises as it cools, and gelatin in particular thickens as the temperature drops.

args.meaning: how strongly a liquid resists flowing
args.boundary: a property of the liquid, not the amount of it

heading: Cooler juice runs out more slowly
narration: Viscosity is a property of the liquid, not the amount of it.

heading: Cooler juice runs out more slowly
narration: The same volume can pour freely when hot and creep when cooler.

heading: Cooler juice runs out more slowly
narration: This is standard physical chemistry, the kind covered in the American Chemical Society's general chemistry resources. A knife cutting a cooler piece is cutting through thicker liquid.

heading: Cooler juice runs out more slowly
narration: A second, less certain part of the explanation is often repeated. As the outer layers cool, the fibres there may relax slightly and hold some of the loose liquid back in the spaces between them.

heading: Cooler juice runs out more slowly
narration: The idea is plausible, but it is harder to isolate in a measurement than viscosity is.

heading: Cooler juice runs out more slowly
narration: Treat it as a possible contributor, not a settled cause. Either way, both effects push in the same direction.

heading: Cooler juice runs out more slowly
narration: A slightly cooler, more evenly heated piece of meat releases its loose liquid more slowly when it is cut, so less of it reaches the board in the first minute.

heading: What to notice in the edit
narration: Watch the sear, which keeps sizzling because it never sealed anything. And notice the one box left open, which is how much resting changes total loss. The answer depends on the cut and the conditions.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: This evidence does not give a single correct resting time for every cut.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: The only time stated in this episode is the USDA's 3-minute rest, and that rest exists for temperature, not for juiciness.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: The evidence does not show that juice migrates to the centre. It also does not show that resting saves most of the liquid that cooking pushes loose, because much of that liquid is gone before the meat leaves the heat.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: It does not settle whether people can taste the difference in a blind comparison.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: Juiciness is partly a sensation, and sensory studies measure people, not water.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: Finally, the carryover rise has no fixed size. Mass, heat and time set its range.

heading: Closing
narration: So the minutes after cooking are not empty. Heat is still crossing the meat from the outside in, and the loose liquid inside it is cooling and thickening.

heading: Closing
narration: Resting is the name for letting both of those finish before the knife decides where the water goes.
